unitObjectives.objective: Pupils will be able to ask and answer prices of everyday and classroom items using 'How much is it? / It is...'
Pupils will be able to identify 6 major historical stages of money on a chronological timeline (barter, cowrie shells, metal tools, coins, paper money, credit cards).
Pupils will be able to identify problem and solution text structures in informational and narrative texts.
Pupils will be able to pronounce, read, and spell words with the 'ar' pattern (/ɑːr/ sound: car, park, hard, farm, card, smart).
Pupils will be able to express moral choices using 'could' and 'should' regarding saving, spending, and helping family.
Pupils will be able to retell the story 'The $100 Bill' using a 5-step narrative frame.

canDo.statement: I can ask how much an item costs.
I can tell the price of an item in dollars or liras.
I can name three things people used as money long ago.
I can read and spell words with 'ar' like car, park, and farm.
I can explain what Paige did with the $100 bill.
I can say what I should do when money is tight.

reading.objective: Follow a chronological timeline and identify problem-solution text structures.

listening.objective: Listen to prices and narrative details to match items with their owners and historical dates.

speaking.objective: Ask and tell prices in a classroom shop role-play and discuss saving versus donating.

writing.objective: Complete a 5-part Story Map and write 3 sentences about a personal problem and solution.

vocabulary.objective: Acquire and use 10 highlighted Words in Context and 16 supporting vocabulary words.

grammar.objective: Use past simple verbs (-ed and irregular) and modals 'could' and 'should' for choices.

phonics.objective: Distinguish and pronounce the /ɑːr/ vowel sound in words.

content.objective: Understand how money evolved historically to make trading and travel easier.

thinking.objective: Sequence historical events in order of time and evaluate good financial choices.

values.objective: Appreciate family effort, generosity over selfishness, and empathy when money is tight.

successCriteria.criterion: Pupil holds up an item and asks 'How much is it?' during pair work.
Pupil orders 'barter', 'cowrie shells', 'metal coins', and 'paper money' correctly on the board.
Pupil correctly spells and blends 'p-ar-k' and 'c-ar-d'.
Pupil states: 'Paige saved the money and took her dad to a restaurant because he was tired.'

readings.title: THE HISTORY OF MONEY
readings.mainIdea: Money evolved from bartering to shells, metal coins, paper notes, and credit cards to make trade easier.
readings.summary: Thousands of years ago, people didn't use money. Instead, they bartered goods like grain for goats. In 1200 BCE, people began using cowrie shells as money. Later in China, people used metal knives and spades, and then round coins with holes. Around 600 BCE, the kings of Lydia made the first true stamped metal coins. Because metal coins were heavy to carry, China invented the first paper money between 800 and 900 CE. In 1958, the first plastic credit card was made. Today, people use electronic money on the internet.

keySentences.sentence: Thousands of years ago, people didn't use money. Instead, people bartered for things they wanted.
However, around 600 BCE, one of the kings of Lydia, which is part of modern-day Turkey, made the first true coins.
The first paper money came from China between 800 and 900 CE. It was easier to carry than metal coins.

2. 1200 BCE: People start using cowrie shells as money.

5. 800-900 CE: China invents the first light paper money.
6. 1958 CE to today: First plastic credit cards and electronic internet payments.

readings.title: THE $100 BILL
readings.mainIdea: Generosity, family love, and seeing parents smile are more valuable than buying expensive material gadgets.
readings.summary: After school, Nina and Jodie laugh at Paige because she does not have a cell phone. Walking home through the park, Paige discovers a wet $100 bill hidden in fallen leaves. She puts the money in her pocket and looks at a beautiful $95 phone in a store window. But she remembers that money is tight at home and decides to save the money. At home, she sees her tired dad in the kitchen. Paige surprises him by inviting him out to a restaurant. Her dad smiles, and Paige feels proud of her kind decision.

keySentences.sentence: "You know I don't have a cell phone." "Oh, Paige! You really should get one!" Jodie laughed hard. Nina laughed too.
She picked it up. A hundred dollars! The bill was wet and dirty. Who did it belong to?
Paige's dad sat in the kitchen. He looked really tired. "Hi, honey," he said, and gave her a hug.

keyFactsTeacherSaysAloud.fact: Thousands of years ago, people didn't use money. Instead, people bartered for things they wanted.
Around 600 BCE, one of the kings of Lydia, which is part of modern-day Turkey, made the first true coins.
The first paper money came from China between 800 and 900 CE because it was easier to carry than heavy metal coins.

Lydia was located in Anatolia near modern Manisa and Salihli, Turkey.

speakingRubric.developing: Uses single isolated words with Turkish prompts; struggles with 'How much is it?'
